highlights.text: عَسَى (ʿasā) means "to yearn for, to hope and expect."
عَسى رَبُّكُمْ أَنْ يُهْلِكَ عَدُوَّكُمْ ("It may be that your Lord will destroy your enemy," 7:129) effectively means "be hopeful of that."
Many Qur'an commentators read the particles لعلّ ("perhaps") and عَسَى in the Qur'an in a non-literal, "binding" sense
whose whole range goes back to a matter involving some difficulty — whether in speech or in anything else.
such a person is مُعْتِب, one who turns back from the wrong.
Of a man who asks to be given satisfaction: قَدِ اسْتَعْتَبَ.
Al-Mutalammis: "He is set upon the hateful ʿatab and is left to dry.
Abū al-Aswad: "So I reproached him, then returned with gentle reproach and well-rooted speech; but I found him neither seeking to make amends nor remembering God save little.
presence and nearness — being at hand, ready.
belongs here in the sense "present/prepared."
أَعْتَدْنَاهُ = "we made it ready, prepared it"
al-Nābigha, on a man whose readiness/resolve distance cannot undo.
Salāma b. Jandal, describing a swift, ready steed.
the root ʿ-t-l signals intensity and physical strength in a thing.
al-ʿutull — a strong, powerfully-built, sound-bodied man.
"Seize him and drag him into the midst of the Blazing Fire," as an instance of this verb (faʿtilūhu, "drag him").
(1) nobility/excellence — of form and of character
(2) oldness/age
This is the root of "al-bayt al-ʿatīq" (the Ancient/Free House), i.e. the Kaʿba — Ibn Fāris quotes Qur'an 22:29 ("let them circle the ancient House")
it was "saved" from the Flood and raised up; saved from the Abyssinians in the Year of the Elephant; or freed from anyone's claim to own it, since it belongs to God.
highlights.note: reported traditional explanations of the Kaʿba's name

highlights.text: A verse of ʿAntara using "al-ʿatīq" is quoted with two rival readings offered by other scholars — a kind of aged dates, or water (called noblest of drinks, "in which is life").
A good wide wineskin is "ʿātiq" (Labīd cites one in a verse)
a sound root whose core sense is arrogance and self-magnification (istikbār).
ʿatā / yaʿtū / ʿutuwwan — "to become arrogant, haughty, overbearing."
so it did not rebel
To discover / come upon something (al-iṭṭilāʿ)
To stir up dust (ithārat al-ghubār)
glossed by Ibn Fāris simply as "if it is discovered."
Causative: aʿthartu fulānan ʿalā kadhā = "I made so-and-so discover/find out about such-and-such.
Cited in verse: "a land abounding in al-ʿāthūr" — meaning a land full of death-traps (matālif), i.e. places of ruin.
ʿātha / yaʿīthu (ʿayth): to move fast and unchecked in doing damage.
Proverbial usage: "you are more destructive to property than the wood-worm in summer.
Abū Dhuʾayb is cited: "so he groped in the quiver, drawing back
taking refuge. عاذ به (ʿādha bihi) = he took refuge with / clung to something for protection;
مَعاذَ الله = "taking refuge in God."
تعوَّذ (taʿawwadha) and استعاذ (istaʿādha) = to seek refuge in God;
أعاذ / عَوَّذ = to grant refuge, to protect.
illustrated with al-Sahmī's verse asking God for protection lest transgressors lead the speaker astray.
birds taking refuge on a protecting mountain (with Bakhdaj's satirical verse; the poet doubles the words ʿiyādhan ʿuwwadhan for emphasis).
(1) doing a thing a second time — returning/repetition
(2) a kind of wood
al-ʿawd is repeating an act, "a return after a beginning" — one says "he began, then returned."
al-maʿād: anything one returns/comes back to (its destination). The Hereafter is a maʿād for people.
"He repeated (aʿāda) the prayer and the speech.
al-ʿīd, a day of assembly/festival: al-Khalīl derives it from ʿāda yaʿūdu (they "return" to it);
shāhid from the poet ʿUbayd/ʿAbīd).
ʿAntara's verse pictures an ostrich that returns to its eggs hourly.
a single sound root whose whole family turns on one idea: a bend in a thing (mayal), or the act of turning/inclining something (mayl).
ʿiwaj (kasra) — crookedness in something spread flat (a carpet), or in an "affair" (amr), such as a dīn (a way one follows) or a maʿāsh (livelihood).
Ruʾba: "my staff bent like a hard, rough branch.
Dhū al-Rumma: she carried him across the waterless waste at a steady gait, "as though, ahead of the other mounts, she were a male ostrich when startled.
What destroys or ruins.
What is burdensome, weighs heavily.

al-ʿawl is abandoning equity by taking more than one's rightful due. He glosses Qur'an 4:3 — "That is nearer to your not committing ʿawl (allā taʿūlū)" — with exactly this sense: not deviating from fairness/justice.
He cites the hadith: "Begin with yourself, then with whomever you support (taʿūlu).
A technical legal use, "ʿālat al-farīḍah": an inheritance share is said to "overrun" when the shares fixed by the text add up to more than the estate can bear.
whereas *ʿām* is used of a year of ease and abundance.
In "he remained among them a thousand sana less fifty ʿām," the larger figure is given with *sana* and the subtracted figure with *ʿām*.
al-Rāghib al-Iṣfahānī groups this root around the idea of aid and mutual support.
"So help me with strength" (18:95)
seeking or asking for help — "Seek help through patience and prayer" (2:45).
Al-ʿāʾiq (العائق) is "that which turns someone away from a good they intend/seek"
Al-Rāghib glosses al-muʿawwiqīn as "those who discourage [others] and turn [them] away from the path of good"
**Root 1 — taking turns, alternation (tadāwul).**
**Root 2 — a defect in one of the two eyes; at base, emptiness of sight.**
On this basis Ibn Fāris explains Q 33:13, "they say our houses are ʿawra, though they are not ʿawra" — glossed as "as though they were not secure."
a place became a ʿawra (vulnerable/exposed); أَعْوَرَ البَيْتُ — a weak point appeared in the house.
Cited verse: do not speak the ʿawrāʾ word heedlessly in company, for someone present will remember it.
"a ʿawrāʾ word was said and I paid it no heed; ʿawrāʾ speech finds no acceptance with me.
Ibn Fāris treats ʿ-Y-SH as one sound root whose single idea is **life and continuing to subsist**.
That by which a person lives: food, drink, and whatever else sustains life.
so it denotes a *way* or *style* of living, not the substance of it.
Q 78:11, "and We made the day a maʿāsh"
"the mainstay of a livelihood, who does not loosen her waist-wrapper;
al-ʿayb / al-ʿaybah / al-ʿāb = a blemish, fault.
The lexicographer Abū al-Haytham glosses the Qurʾanic verse "so I intended to make it defective" (Q18:79, about the boat in Sūrat al-Kahf) as "to give it a fault,"
A verse plays on this: "I am the man you faulted — yet no fault-finder can find a fault in him.
"my companion is good-humored, neither faulty nor a faultfinder").
A hadith calls the Anṣār "my ʿaybah and my karish [inner circle]," meaning his intimates and confidants.
A hadith from the Ḥudaybiya peace treaty between the Prophet and the Meccans describes the pact as "an ʿaybah makfūfa" (a bag tied shut)

A hadith about ʿĀʾisha and the Prophet's oath of withdrawal (īlāʾ) from his wives: when ʿUmar blamed her, she retorted, "What business is it of yours, Ibn al-Khaṭṭāb — mind your own household (ʿaybatik)!
**Core sense: poverty / neediness.**
Q9:28, {wa-in khiftum ʿaylatan} — "and if you fear poverty."
The verb: ʿāla yaʿīlu ʿaylatan — "he became poor / fell into need."
"mā ʿāla muqtaṣid" — "one who spends moderately never becomes poor.
"man ʿāla minnā baʿdahā fa-lā anjabar"
a single sound root whose core meaning is "an organ by which one sees and looks" (the eye).
Citing al-Khalīl: al-ʿayn is the seeing organ of any creature with sight.
A water-spring (al-ʿayn) — the welling spring, named for likeness to the eye in clarity and water.
citing {wa-ḥūrun ʿīnun…} (al-Wāqiʿa 22), which he glosses only as "wide-eyed ones, like guarded pearls," without importing further meaning.
he insists ʿayyin means "full of holes/thin spots" (even a new skin can have holes from a hide-defect), citing al-Qaṭāmī as proof.
(I) a thing jutting out and rising up
(II) coming and going
the ass, wild or domestic
Taʾabbaṭa Sharran, on a night halt where nothing detained him "but the unburdening of a mount, and an eye I wrestle with lest it sleep"
al-Ḥārith b. Ḥillizah, "everyone who strikes the ʿayr is an ally of ours" — glossed as everyone whose eyelid blinks over the pupil.
Q 50:15 'Were We incapacitated/wearied by the first creation?'
Ibn Fāris gives this root one core sense: distancing and withdrawal.
anything that escapes your grasp is said to have "ʿazaba'd from you."
meaning "to set aside" and "to turn or lean away."
عَزَلَ (ʿazala, "he set [a thing] aside"), imperfect yaʿzilu = to move it off to one side.
العُزلة (al-ʿuzla) = seclusion, i.e. withdrawing oneself (al-iʿtizāl).
"the milch-camels of the solitary, aloof one (al-miʿzāl).
no skulkers-aside in the wars, but rather men bare [of armor]
Ibn Fāris treats ʿ-z-m as a single sound root whose core idea is **ṣarīma and qaṭʿ** — a settled severing, a cutting through.
ʿazama / yaʿzimu / ʿazm — to resolve, i.e. to cut a matter through.
ʿazm is "what the heart is knotted upon, of a matter you are going to do" — something you are certain of.
This severance reading of ulū al-ʿazm is Ibn Fāris's own derivation from qaṭʿ, not a sense the verse itself spells out.
